newsitem.title: UK: Copper ends weak on LME, spreads partly unravelled.
newsitem.headline: Copper ends weak on LME, spreads partly unravelled.

text.p: Copper prices dived to the lowest levels since January 7 during Wednesday afternoon LME trading, with the market unnerved by a contraction in some spread backwardations from February onwards.
Other metals were hit to some extent by the losses in copper, with the exchange suffering a "down day", although the declines were only of note in aluminium and lead, traders said.
"Copper took a bit of a pasting when the spreads softened, and there were some stops hit when it broke $2,220 and $2,200. Some of the specs baled out then," one trader said.

Today LME Chief Executive David King said the exchange was closly monitoring the copper market, particularly with regard to the nearby backwardation. This also contributed to the unsettled price trend.

Current tightness is fierce, with cash/one day still at $22/23 backwardation, although cash/threes eased to $245/250 from $335 on Tuesday. February/March narrowed on general lending to $16 from levels of $29 yesterday, calming concern over the February prompt when pricing for the "third Wednesday" takes place.

Fundamentally, news that workers at Chile's Enami had agreed a five-year deal also removed a prop of possible supply disruption. Meanwhile, earlier in the session South Korea's LG Metals said its LME short positions were a carryover hedge, it had not requested increased credit lines, nor had it received margin calls from brokers.
There has been widespread concern recently over this company's activities, as many traders believe they are one of the shorts being hurt by the backwardation.
Three months hit a low of $2,178 a tonne before concluding the kerb at $2,183, a $61 loss from yesterday. Prices may bounce back above $2,200, or slide further to $2,150.
"Its an old cliche, but you just cannot call the next $50 in this market," another trader said.

Aluminium was depressed by negative charts after a recent double failure at $1,640, and dropped under liquidation to near $1,600 at one point. Last business was at $1,613, down $19, with the market needing to regain $1,625 to head off further losses.

Lead dived to the lowest levels since October 1995 during the kerb, as bearish sentiment from copper cascaded through the market. Also, the fundamental picture is not exciting in the short-term, as winter - the peak period for replacement battery demand - draws on.
Last business was at $669 a tonne, down $6 from Tuesday, but above a $662 low. Technicians see the market ranging down to $640/650.
Zinc slithered down to a low-point of $1,120 at one stage, although the selling pressure was not so intense. Last trade was at $1,126, down $4 from yesterday.
Nickel trading was erratic, although the market was well defended on dips towards $7,150. However, the overall direction was downwards, and last trade was at $7,180, down $40.

Tin retreated to the $5,800 level, but was supported here, albeit in fairly low-key trading. Final business was at this level, down $75 from Tuesday, with more losses likely as physical interest is said to be running at a low ebb.
The alloy market was hurt by the decline in primary prices, and fell to $1,505 on the kerb, down from yesterday's close of $1,535/40.
